content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a gas-powered mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users can manually drive the machine along the lawn's edge to build a virtual map. Once set up, the machine will automatically mow according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think for many people this one may be easier to use.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how the two machines understand your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the perimeter with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map the lawn, with no need to bury boundary wires or install a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method of building the initial map takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who aren't very tech-savvy.

To verify this claim, I had my mum, who lives in another state, install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She reported back that everything worked fine. But I'm not entirely sure whether she had the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire perimeter with her iPhone and then mark out every area that needed to be avoided.

The automatic mapping did cause one small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map.

I marked that area as a no-go zone in the app and the problem was solved. That said, if there's no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, you'll need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping.

A peek through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also deliver one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could sit indoors working while watching, from the mower's perspective, as it moved around the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun to use and sometimes helps explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps have quite a lot in common. Both support scheduled jobs, mowing mode adjustments, zone划分, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly nice variation on the last feature. In addition to the traditional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically on a preset schedule without any intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick mode is a lot of fun for clearing up small patches it missed.

Sometimes, I almost feel like I'm telepathically controlling the robot (the fun kind of telepathy, that is). I walk alongside the mower, iPhone in hand, barely moving my thumb, and the machine is already following my direction.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder in operation.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow 'noisy', but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly—quiet enough that it's easy to forget it's still going, including when it uses its headlight to mow after dark.

Because TerraMow relies on camera-based navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. So scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow performs reliably. I've relied on it for weeks on end without needing to step in to handle routine mowing.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can occasionally backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you can't perform other operations in the app.

After several days of continuous rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. One area of the yard had standing water, and TerraMow reasonably avoided that area on its next run.

Inside the skipped circular patch, the weeds grew taller. Over time, the mower似乎 came to treat that growth as an object to keep avoiding, and even after the ground dried out, the area was still ignored.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive the mower over and clear the taller grass, and the problem was solved. Once that area returned to a normal appearance, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging can also help TerraMow reach its boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing along模糊 boundary lines might otherwise be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids the map 'changing its mind' about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac conclusion

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward TerraMow's camera-based approach.

Burying boundary wires was a complete non-starter for me, and installing an RTK base station meant extra hardware to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. Initial map building takes longer, invisible property lines require manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are still manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, an engaging live camera view, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I've used.

I do enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that job over to a robot frees up my time for landscaping, edging, and detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does this well enough that I'd recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower but doesn't want to bury boundary wires, install an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard with a phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently lists the TerraMow V1000 at $999 after applying a $200 coupon on the site. It's also available on TerraMow's official website.
